en.title: GTA 6's Secret Zombie Shooter Minigame Offers Hours of Roguelike Mayhem
en.summary: Forget the advertised thrills; Grand Theft Auto VI hides a surprisingly deep, addictive zombie shooter minigame. This isn't just a quick diversion, but a full-blown arcade experience that could consume hours of your playtime.
en.body:
While the neon-drenched Vice City and its sprawling open world are rightfully grabbing headlines, Grand Theft Auto VI harbors a secret that might just steal the show for many players. Buried within the game, accessible through an in-game console, lies **Street Trash 3: Dezombifier**, an isometric twin-stick shooter that IGN reports is so compelling, it could easily become the game's most addictive minigame. This isn't a simple arcade distraction; it's a robust experience inspired by titles like **Dead Nation**, but with a modern roguelike deckbuilder twist.

Players, taking on the role of Jason, find themselves headshotting hordes of undead nightmares. Each fallen foe rewards players with XP, crucial for leveling up. At each level-up, a choice of cards is presented, allowing players to strategically enhance their build. These cards range from basic stat boosts like increased movement speed and fire rate to game-changing abilities that can double damage output at the cost of taking more hits. The ultimate goal is to collect six scattered gears across a deceptively large map and escape via a rooftop chopper, a task made challenging by frequent deaths that nevertheless provide vital learning opportunities about the map layout and available card synergies.

## The Strategy of Survival

The true magic of **Street Trash 3** lies in its on-the-fly build crafting and the satisfying spiral of power it creates. Much like the addictive loop found in **Vampire Survivors**, the game encourages players to lean into specific playstyles. One successful strategy might involve focusing on rapid-fire weapons, like swapping a pistol for a micro-SMG and buffing fire rate to create a bullet stream. Alternatively, players could invest in speed and stamina, enabling them to outrun and outmaneuver massive enemy groups. The emergent gameplay, driven by the cards dealt and player choices, ensures that no two runs are quite the same, offering significant replayability within the game itself.

## Beyond the Main Story

The sheer depth of this minigame is already sparking conversations within the player community. While **Grand Theft Auto VI** is being lauded by many as the 'best game ever made' for its stunning graphics, ambitious open-world design, and compelling narrative, it's these unexpected, fully-realized diversions that truly showcase Rockstar's dedication to player experience. The ability to dive into other, fully-formed video games within the world of GTA is a testament to their meticulous attention to detail, offering players more than just the main quest to sink their teeth into. This hidden gem promises hours of challenging fun, proving that sometimes, the greatest adventures are found off the beaten path.

## What's Next

As players continue to explore the vast world of **Grand Theft Auto VI**, discovering these hidden minigames will undoubtedly become a significant part of the experience. Further details on other in-game activities and their complexities are expected to emerge as the community delves deeper into Rockstar's latest masterpiece.

content_raw: To say I was up until midnight last night with GTA 6 is technically correct, but not the full picture. What I was actually doing was headshotting undead nightmares in Street Trash 3: Dezombifier, a moreish isometric twin-stick shooter that lives inside Jason's PS5-alike JoySystem. You play it briefly with Cal during the story, and it impressed me enough to want to beat it fully. After nearly four hours, I still haven't. It's clearly inspired by the Sony-published Dead Nation from 2010, but it mashes the zombie slaying with a roguelike deckbuilder. Every time an enemy squelches, their blood splattering the pavement, you gain XP, and at each new level you pick a card to adjust your build. Basic cards boost movement speed, fire rate, damage or critical hit chance, but rarer cards transform your tactics, such as one that doubles your damage given and received. Your goal is to collect six gears strewn around a deceptively large map and leave via a rooftop chopper. You'll die a lot, but on each run you'll learn a little more about the world's layout and discover new cards to experiment with. The satisfaction of Street Trash 3 is in crafting a build on the fly from the cards you're dealt, and in feeling your power spiral. You're constantly levelling up and that escalation, the way your build rapidly grows and branches depending on what you find, reminds me a lot of Vampire Survivors . Like that game, it's most fun when you lean into a specific skill: the closest I've come to victory was when I swapped my pistol for a micro-SMG, buffing and buffing my fire rate until the bullets streamed like a deadly snake. I also got deep on a run boosting my speed and stamina so I could infinitely sprint from groups of enemies, and another where – inspired by a detailed Reddit thread discussing the best builds – I found a card that improved my critical chance by 50% while standing still. When combined with other critical hit cards, I could basically stand in the same spot and mow down everything down around me, painting a gruesome circle of guts. There is so much craft that most players simply won't see, so many developer hours spent creating missable moments of delight. It is ludicrous that something as meaty and polished as Street Trash 3 exists inside another video game – and even more ludicrous that it's one of three games you can play on Jason's console (Rockstar told Kotaku that "an internal dev team within the dev team" makes these games). But, like in real life, not every game available for the JoySystem is a banger. Of the three games on Jason’s hard drive, Time Jackers Rewind is the most forgettable. It's a stylish top-down shooter that plays a bit like a slower, sci-fi, less-good Hotline Miami . I appreciate how its checkpoints are tantalizingly spread far enough that you can't just sprint between them, close enough that after every death I was sure I was seconds away.
